dataframe is a library of labelled, columnar tables for Go notebooks and programs: a Series is one typed column with an Index of row labels, a DataFrame is named columns sharing one index. It is pure Go (CGO=0), sits on go-ndarray for numbers, and takes pandas as its behavioural reference: where it answers the same question, it gives pandas’ answer, and every place it does not is listed below, on purpose.
data.algorithms#Algorithms: Hashing and keys. Group-by, merge, alignment, IsIn, Unique and ValueCounts all reduce to one primitive, joint factorisation: code the key tuples of one or two tables into dense integers (jointCodes). One int64 key whose values span a range no wider than a few times the row count is coded with a lookup table instead of a hash map (the common case of small integer keys); otherwise each key column is factorised with a Go map of its element type and the per-key codes are combined, compacting when the combined space would overflow. Group-by codes the keys once, sorts only the groups (not the rows) to get pandas’ sort=True order, then aggregates in one pass per column with per-group accumulators (sum, count, mean, var/std two-pass), or by picking one row per group (min, max, first, last), which keeps the dtype. Sorting is stable and LSD: one stable pass per key, least significant first. A pass over a float64, int64 (also datetime and period) or int32 key is a radix sort on an order-preserving uint64 image of the key (11-bit digits, skipping digits all keys share); other dtypes use a merge sort with the dtype’s comparison. Missing values go last for every key. Merge factorises both sides’ keys jointly, buckets the right rows by code, and emits row pairs in pandas’ order; then gathers every column once. Gathers (take) run in parallel over row chunks for large columns, and frames gather their columns concurrently.
data.arrow-and-parquet-design#Arrow and Parqu:
Two packages move frames in and out of Apache Arrow data:
arrowio converts frames to and from Arrow record batches and tables, and reads and writes Arrow IPC (the file format, also called Feather v2, and the streaming format). parquetio reads and writes Parquet. It reuses arrowio’s public conversions (ToRecord, FromTable) and adds only the Parquet layer. Parquet is a separate package so that a program that only needs IPC does not link Parquet and gRPC (see “Binary size” below). This note records which Arrow implementation both are built on, why, what that costs, and how the types and the index map.
data.columns#Columns:
A column is one generic implementation, col[T], over a storage element type T, plus a small table of per-dtype operations (ops[T]: ordering, formatting, boxing to a Go value, recognising NaN). Writing the column machinery once and instantiating it per element type keeps the hot loops monomorphic (a gather over []float64 is a gather over []float64, not over []any) and keeps the code small enough to hold to 100% statement coverage.
dtype storage notes float64, float32, int8…int64, uint8…uint64, bool, complex64, complex128 a go-ndarray array the same 13 dtypes as go-ndarray, in its order string []string datetime int64 nanoseconds since the epoch, UTC, in an ndarray pandas’ datetime64[ns] category int32 codes in an ndarray + the category labels categories are sorted when inferred period int64 ordinals + a frequency Y, Q, M, W, D, h, min, s Numeric columns are go-ndarray arrays. A column that owns its storage allocates it inside an ndarray.Array (ZerosOf then Data[T], which returns the backing slice), so Series.Values() hands the array out without copying, and arithmetic is done by go-ndarray (Add, Sub, Mul, Div, AsType), which gives NumPy’s type promotion for free. A column that is a slice of another (Head, Iloc(Slice(...))) shares the parent’s storage and copies only if Values() is asked for.
Missing values are a validity bitmap, one bit per row, nil when every value is present (the common case costs nothing). For float columns NaN also counts as missing, as in pandas, so data that arrives with NaN behaves as expected. Every dtype can be missing, including integers and bools.
Columns and frames are immutable: operations return new values and share whatever they did not change (renaming, selecting columns, SetIndex copy no data). This removes pandas’ view-versus-copy questions (SettingWithCopyWarning) by construction.

data.deliberate-differences-from-pandas#Delib:
Each is exercised by the fixture tests, which allow exactly these differences and no other.
Integer and bool columns keep their dtype when values are missing. pandas turns an int64 column with a missing value into float64 (NaN), and a bool one into object; here they stay int64/bool with a validity bitmap — what pandas calls its nullable Int64/boolean dtypes. This shows up after merge (unmatched rows), reindex, concat with a missing column, unstack, shift, and in CSV columns with empty fields. Missing integers print as . Column labels are strings. pandas allows any hashable; T() and Unstack name columns by the formatted labels. Several aggregations of one column are named column_func (e.g. x_sum), where pandas makes a two-level column index. A column with a single aggregation keeps its name. Aggregations are numeric_only. Sum, Mean, Std, Var, Median of a frame or a group-by skip non-numeric columns (pandas concatenates strings for sum and raises for mean); Min, Max, First, Last, Count, NUnique take every column in group-by, and numeric ones in frame reductions. Describe skips bool columns, as pandas does. Sorting is always stable (pandas’ kind="stable"); pandas’ default quicksort may order ties differently. No object dtype. A transpose or melt of mixed columns gives string columns; Concat of incompatible columns (int and string) is an error where pandas makes an object column. Instants are UTC nanoseconds. Time-zone offsets in parsed strings are applied, and the result is UTC (pandas keeps a tz-aware dtype). Out-of-range instants (before 1677 or after 2262) are an error, as pandas’ OutOfBoundsDatetime. Date parsing is per element. ToDatetime reads ISO 8601 and a list of common layouts element by element; pandas infers one format from the first element and fails on a different one. Month-first is assumed for 01/02/2024, as pandas does by default. Resampling supports fixed bins (s, min, h, D with a count, origin at midnight of the first day) and calendar bins W, ME, QE, YE, MS, QS, YS with a count of one. Other rules (business days, anchored offsets other than Sunday weeks, closed/label overrides) are not implemented. A boolean mask series must cover the frame’s labels. Like pandas, a mask with another index is aligned by label; a frame label the mask lacks is an error (pandas raises too). Join with overlapping column names needs suffixes, as pandas. Rolling windows are by row count only (no time-based windows) and are computed directly per window (O(n·w)).
data.deliberate-differences-from-pandas-1#Del:
Each of these is checked by the corpus test, which names the rule that applied to each column (D1–D7); everything else must match pandas 3.0.6 exactly, values and dtypes, and WriteCSV must write byte for byte what to_csv writes for every frame read identically (47 of the 69 cases).
D1 — integers with missing values stay int64. pandas makes such a column float64 with NaN (losing exactness above 2^53); ours is Int64 with a validity bitmap, the equivalent of pandas’ nullable Int64. D2 — bools with missing values stay bool, with a validity bitmap (pandas: object). D3 — uint64 with missing values stays uint64, with a validity bitmap (pandas: text, keeping the missing-value tokens as text). D4 — parse_dates reads each value on its own. Any ISO 8601 form (date, date and time, fractional seconds, Z or an offset, which is applied) and a list of common layouts are accepted per value; pandas 3 infers one format from the first value and leaves the column as text when another value differs (2020-01-01 then 2020-01-02 10:00). A value that is no date leaves the column text in both. Instants are naive UTC nanoseconds: a Z or offset is converted to UTC (pandas: a tz-aware dtype), and the unit is always ns (pandas 3 infers one, e.g. us). D5 — integers beyond 64 bits stay text (String; pandas: object holding Python ints). D6 — floats are correctly rounded, as pandas’ float_precision= "round_trip" reads them. pandas’ default parser can be one ulp off, and reads 0.30000000000000004 as 0.3; the corpus compares our floats with pandas’ round-trip parse. D7 — an explicit int or bool dtype accepts missing values (validity bitmap); pandas raises “Integer column has NA values”. Differences outside what the corpus can show:
Text columns are String; a column with no rows (header only, nrows=0) is String where pandas says object. Error messages count lines from 1: pandas’ “EOF inside string starting at row 2” is our “EOF inside string starting at line 3”. Too-many-fields errors give the same line number as pandas (“expected 2 fields in line 4, saw 3”). Errors wrap ErrParse, ErrColumn, ErrIndex, ErrArgument. An explicit Bool dtype also accepts 1 and 0 (pandas does for a column of only those). Duplicate CSVNames are an error, as in pandas. Not supported: index_col lists or False, usecols by position or callable, skiprows as a list or callable, header rows other than the first (use CSVSkipRows), per-column na_values, matching numeric missing values by value (-999 does not match -999.0), thousands, decimal, escapechar, dayfirst, converters, chunksize, compression, and encodings other than UTF-8. Writer: the line end is "\n" on every platform (pandas: os.linesep); float32 columns are written with float32’s shortest digits under Python’s repr rule (1000000.0; pandas/NumPy write 1e+06); complex numbers are written as Go formats them ((1+2i), pandas (1+2j)); an int column with missing values is written as integers (pandas, holding floats, writes 1.0).
data.errors#Errors: Fallible operations return an error wrapping one of the package’s sentinel errors (ErrColumn, ErrLabel, ErrDType, ErrLength, …), to test with errors.Is. Operations that cannot fail (Head, Copy, Describe) return the value alone. Must turns an (v, err) pair into v for notebook cells and examples.
data.how-data-moves#How data moves:
Write: ToRecord shares the frame’s storage. Numeric and datetime columns are wrapped as Arrow buffers without copying (memory.NewBufferBytes over the column’s own slice). Validity bitmaps are re-encoded word by word. Bools are bit-packed, and strings are copied once into one offsets buffer and one data buffer. Read: each column is decoded straight into a fresh ndarray that the new series then owns. There is one copy and no boxing. Validity bitmaps are copied whole with bitutil.CopyBitmap, at any chunk offset. The strings of each chunk are copied into one Go string that every value then slices. The frame never points into Arrow buffers, so it outlives the record and is safe whatever allocator was used. To make this possible without boxing, the core gained four small public entry points (interop.go):
NewSeriesBitmap(name, data, validity []uint64) and (*Series).ValidityBitmap() move a packed validity bitmap in and out. The words are LSB-first, which is the Arrow bit order read as little-endian words. NewCategorical(name, codes, categories) and (*Series).Categorical() move a categorical column as codes plus categories.
data.how-the-reader-works#How the reader work: Whole input in memory. A file is read with parallel ReadAt calls straight into one buffer (which also spreads the page faults of fresh memory over the cores); any other reader through io.ReadAll. A UTF-8 byte order mark is skipped. Header first, serially. Skipped rows, the header and the first data row are tokenized one record at a time; the first data row’s field count decides an implicit index (more fields than names), as in pandas. Speculative parallel tokenizing. The rest is cut into about 4×GOMAXPROCS chunks (at least 1 MiB) at line ends. Each chunk is tokenized on its own as if it began a record. Stitching them in order checks that guess: a chunk is kept only if the previous chunk’s last record ended exactly at its start; otherwise (it began inside a quoted field spanning lines) it is tokenized again from where that record truly ends, or dropped when that record covers it. Correct on every input; as parallel as the input allows. The randomized test TestCSVChunkedMatchesSerial and the corpus run at chunk sizes 1–21 bytes check it. Fields are offsets. A record stores its start and the end of each of its fields as uint32 offsets from the chunk start (a field starts one byte after the previous one ends; a field a short row lacks is marked). No field is copied. Two-pass column conversion, in parallel per column × chunk. The first pass parses integers — or, once a float shows up, floats — straight into the column’s final storage, allocated with makeCol so it is born inside an ndarray and Values() is zero-copy, and records which kinds of value the chunk holds. The kinds of all chunks decide the dtype from the whole column, as pandas decides it. A second pass converts only the chunks whose first pass did not already produce that dtype (an integer chunk of a float column is converted by float64(int64), which rounds as parsing the digits would, except for -0, read again). Integers use a hand-written parser; floats a Clinger fast path (exact mantissa below 2^53, power of ten up to 22) and strconv.ParseFloat otherwise, so every float is correctly rounded. Strings are views. An unquoted field, and a quoted one without doubled quotes, becomes a string pointing into the input buffer (unsafe.String); the buffer is never written after reading. Only fields with doubled quotes, or text after a closing quote, are copied.
data.index#Index:
An Index is either a range (nothing stored: start + i*step), or one or more label columns of any dtype (one: an ordinary or datetime index; several: a multi-level index such as GroupBy over several keys produces). Lookup by label builds a hash map once, lazily, under a sync.Once, so an index is safe to share between goroutines.
Taking rows of a range index keeps it a range when the positions are an arithmetic progression (Head, Tail, Iloc(Slice)), and gives an int64 label index otherwise, as pandas does.
data.memory-trade-off#Memory trade-off:
Zero-copy strings make string columns cost 16 bytes per value plus nothing, and make the reader fast, but any string kept alive keeps the whole input buffer alive: a frame of one short string column read from a 500 MB file holds 500 MB. In the benchmark (docs/perf.md (CSV section)) the frame read from a 497 MB file holds about 1 GB of Go heap (the input, the 16-byte string headers of two string columns, three numeric columns), against 370 MB for polars, which stores strings in Arrow buffers. The peak resident memory during the read is about the same as pandas’ and polars’. A caller who keeps only a small string column for long should copy it (for example AsType(Category)); an option to copy strings into a compact per-column buffer is a possible addition.
Fields are indexed with uint32 offsets from their chunk’s start, so a single record longer than 4 GiB is an error rather than silently wrong.
data.not-done#Not done: Dropping gRPC from Parquet programs. That needs an upstream change that stops pqarrow importing arrow/flight. Reading row groups or columns selectively, and reading in batches. ReadParquet reads the whole file. Read types beyond the mapping: date32/64, decimals, durations, nested types, string_view, and non-string dictionaries. Zero-copy read. The core cannot adopt foreign memory. Its arrays are go-ndarray arrays, and go-ndarray has no exported wrap-without-copy constructor. One copy per column remains. loong64 was cross-built and vetted only, not run.
data.notebook-display#Notebook display: DataFrame, Series and Index have Display() map[string][]byte, which go-notebook shows: text/plain laid out exactly as pandas prints (checked against pandas’ own repr on eight fixtures: column alignment, the leading space convention, float precision with a shared number of decimals, scientific notation when it would hide digits, truncation to 5+5 rows past 60 rows and 10+10 columns past 20, sparsified multi-level indexes, index names on their own line) and text/html, a table like pandas’ notebook one. The limits are package variables (MaxRows, MinRows, MaxColumns).
data.query#Query: DataFrame.Query evaluates a small expression language — columns, @vars, literals, arithmetic, comparisons (chained), in/not in, and/or/not and &/|/~, isna/notna/abs — by a recursive-descent parser that computes as it parses, with vectorised series operations. Nothing is ever executed as code: the grammar is the whole of what an expression can do.
data.the-index#The index:
The "pandas" schema metadata is followed in both directions.
On write:
A range index becomes a range descriptor {kind: range, start, stop, step, name}, and no column. Any other index becomes one column per level, after the data columns. Each is named after its level, or __index_level_k__ when the level is unnamed, and listed in index_columns. The column entries carry pandas_type/numpy_type, so pandas restores categories, zones and nullable dtypes. WithoutIndex drops the index, like pandas’ index=False. On read:
A descriptor start=0, step=1 gives a range index, keeping its name. Any other range gives an int64 labelled index with the same labels. The core’s range index always starts at 0 with step 1. Index columns become the levels of a (multi-)index. Level names come from the metadata, where null means unnamed. Without metadata the frame gets a range index. Malformed metadata is ErrMetadata. pandas 3.0.6 with pyarrow 26.0.0 reads back the files arrowio and parquetio write with the right dtypes and index. It was checked on every format and every kind of index: range, named, multi-level with an unnamed level, stepped range, and datetime.
This check is manual, because it needs Python, and does not run in CI:
DATAFRAME_READBACK_DIR=/tmp/rb go test -run WriteReadback ./parquetio uv run --with pandas --with numpy --with pyarrow \ python parquetio/testdata/check_readback.py /tmp/rb The test is skipped unless the variable is set. The script exits non-zero on any dtype, index or cross-format difference.
data.type-mapping#Type mapping:
dtype written as read from float64, float32 double, float double, float int8..int64, uint8..uint64 same width same width bool bool bool string utf8 (large_utf8 past 2 GiB) utf8, large_utf8; null type (an all-None object column) datetime timestamp[ns, tz=UTC] (WithTimeZone) timestamp[s, ms, us or ns], any zone category dictionary dictionary period utf8, its text (Series.Strings) n/a complex64/128 ErrUnsupported n/a Anything else on read is ErrUnsupported: lists, structs, decimals, dates, durations, and dictionaries of non-strings.
Missing values use the validity bitmaps in both directions. A float column marks missing values in band with NaN, as pandas does.
On write, NaN becomes null, which is also what pandas writes. On read, a null float becomes NaN. Arrow distinguishes a non-null NaN from null, but our model cannot, so both read as missing. A null in any other column becomes a masked value. In the pandas metadata, an integer or bool column with a mask is described with pandas’ nullable dtype (Int64, UInt16, boolean, …). pandas then reads it back as nullable instead of casting it to float. Datetimes are UTC instants.
Writing tags them “UTC” by default. pandas then reads datetime64[ns, UTC]. WithTimeZone("") writes naive timestamps, which pandas reads as datetime64[ns]. On read, the zone is ignored: Arrow stores UTC instants whatever the zone. A naive timestamp is taken as UTC wall time. Coarser units are scaled to nanoseconds. A value outside the nanosecond range (years 1677 to 2262) is ErrOutOfRange. Periods are written as text. Arrow has no calendar-period type, and the pandas period extension type is pyarrow-specific. The core has no public period constructor yet, so this path is untested with real periods. It is the same code path as strings.
data.which-implementation#Which implementatio:
Three candidates were examined (versions of 2026-10-10).
github.com/go-ruby-arrow/arrow and github.com/go-ruby-parquet/parquet. These are reimplementations of the Ruby surface of the red-arrow and red-parquet gems. Their README says so directly: “It does not reimplement the columnar format; it re-presents arrow-go through Ruby’s naming and semantics.” Reading the source confirms it. arrow (1,333 lines) wraps apache/arrow-go/v18 arrays, schemas, tables and IPC behind Ruby-shaped types. Values go in and out boxed, one any per value (NewArrayOf(dt, []any), Array.Get(i) any, ToSlice() []any). parquet (694 lines) is a bridge from pqarrow to those Ruby-shaped tables. Neither has a format core that could be reused. Using them would mean using arrow-go through a boxing layer built for an interpreter. At 10^6 to 10^7 rows, boxing every value costs more than the whole conversion. Their go.mod files also show that they bring in exactly the dependencies of arrow-go. Not used. The fleet’s own work points the same way: both modules build on arrow-go.
github.com/apache/arrow-go/v18 v18.8.0, the Apache Arrow project’s own Go implementation. Used.
Pure Go. The only cgo in the packages we link (arrow, arrow/array, arrow/ipc, arrow/memory, parquet, parquet/file, parquet/pqarrow, parquet/compress) is the optional C allocator, which sits behind the cgo && ccalloc build tags. go list -deps with CGO_ENABLED=1 finds no package with cgo files in our dependency graph. The default allocator is the Go allocator. SIMD kernels exist for amd64 and arm64, and every other architecture has a pure-Go fallback.
Endianness. arrow-go keeps buffers in native byte order, and its IPC reader swaps a file written on a machine of the other order. Its Parquet encoders write little-endian on every machine.
Compression codecs, all pure Go:
Snappy and Gzip: klauspost/compress Zstd: klauspost/compress/zstd LZ4: pierrec/lz4/v4 (LZ4_RAW in Parquet, LZ4 frames in IPC) Brotli: andybalholm/brotli The parquet/compress package registers all of them, so all of them are linked whichever one is used.
Other dependencies linked:
Parquet metadata: apache/thrift IPC messages: google/flatbuffers hashing: zeebo/xxh3, cespare/xxhash also google/uuid and goccy/go-json CPU feature detection: klauspost/cpuid golang.org/x/exp, golang.org/x/sync, golang.org/x/sys pqarrow imports arrow/flight just to (de)serialise the stored Arrow schema (flight.SerializeSchema/DeserializeSchema). That one import links gRPC and protobuf: 64 grpc packages, plus x/net/http2. Binary size. These are stripped linux/amd64 binaries that write one frame:
program size the core alone 2.0 MB arrow-go IPC only (no arrowio) 4.7 MB arrow-go parquet/file only 20.2 MB using arrowio (IPC writer) 7.7 MB using parquetio (Parquet writer) 32.9 MB Before the split, when Parquet lived in arrowio, the IPC-only program weighed 29.9 MB. Now it links no parquet package and no gRPC package (checked with go list -deps). The Parquet program links 15 arrow-go parquet packages and 64 grpc packages.
Architectures. The test binaries were checked on every target.
go vet ./... and go test -c of arrowio and parquetio (with CGO_ENABLED=0) pass for linux/{amd64, arm64, s390x, ppc64le, riscv64, loong64} and windows/amd64. The full arrowio and parquetio suites were run on linux/s390x, ppc64le, riscv64 and amd64 under qemu-user, through Docker Desktop’s binfmt handlers, and passes on all four. That includes the pandas fixtures, which are little-endian files. A probe binary confirmed that the s390x run really was big-endian. Files written on s390x were read by pandas on the host and came out equal to the ones written on arm64. linux/arm64 ran natively. loong64 has no binfmt handler on this host (exec format error), so for loong64 the code is only built and vetted, not run. The alternative to arrow-go was to write our own Arrow IPC and Parquet codecs. That means flatbuffers and Thrift metadata, five codecs, and the Parquet encodings and definition levels. It is thousands of lines that arrow-go already maintains upstream and tests against the other Arrow implementations. Reuse wins.

data:
DataFrame, Series and Index have Display(), which returns the value in every format a notebook front end may show, keyed by MIME type: text/plain (what String prints, laid out as pandas prints it) and text/html (the table pandas shows in a notebook). It is the display contract of the go-notebook kernel, so a cell whose last expression is a frame shows it as a table.
Every output on this page was produced by go-dataframe v0.1.0 from the code shown above it: figures/.go in this site’s repository writes it, and the CI writes it again and fails if one byte differs.

data: All numbers are wall-clock medians of interleaved runs (Go, then pandas and polars, repeated), on an Apple M4 Max (16 cores, 128 GB), macOS, Go 1.27.2, pandas 3.0.6, polars (latest from PyPI via uv), numpy 2.5. The host is shared and was loaded by other work throughout (uptime load averages are given for each run); treat differences under ~1.5x as noise, and the polars column especially, since polars is multi-threaded too and suffers most from a busy machine.
data.arrow-and-parquet-performance#Arrow and: All measurements write and read a 10^6-row frame in memory, comparing arrowio (IPC) and parquetio (Parquet) with pandas (pyarrow engine). They were taken on 2026-10-10.
data.conditions#Conditions: Apple M4 Max, 16 cores, 128 GB, macOS 26.6.2; Go 1.27.2; pandas 3.0.6, polars 2.0.0, pyarrow (pandas’ engine="pyarrow"), Python 3.12.12. The machine was shared and loaded: load average 14–16 for most runs, rising to 45 during the last (10^7 rows, dates) series. Every reader ran under the same load, but absolute times are pessimistic and the spread is wide; the ratios are the meaningful part. Table: id (int64), x (standard normal, full 17-digit precision), y (two decimals), cat (cat0..cat49), date (YYYY-MM-DD), as written by pandas’ to_csv. 10^6 rows = 49 MB, 10^7 rows = 497 MB. Method: each read in its own process under /usr/bin/time -l; each process times only the read call (warm page cache, no process start-up). The readers run interleaved (ours, pandas C, pandas pyarrow, polars, ours, …), 5 rounds; the table gives the median (min–max). “Data MB”: Go heap live after the read and a GC (runtime.MemStats. HeapAlloc), pandas memory_usage(deep=True).sum(), polars estimated_size(). These are not quite the same measure: ours includes the input buffer the string columns point into (see the memory trade-off in docs/design.md (CSV section)). “Peak RSS”: maximum resident set size of the whole process. The Python processes include ~118 MB for the interpreter and the imports alone.
data.csv-reader-performance#CSV reader perfor: Measured 2026-10-10 with bench/csv/bench.py (reproduce with the command in its docstring; the data files go to a temporary directory outside the repository).
data.how-to-rerun#How to rerun: go test -c -o /tmp/arrowio.test ./arrowio go test -c -o /tmp/parquetio.test ./parquetio for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7; do /tmp/parquetio.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 3x /tmp/arrowio.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 3x (cd arrowio/testdata && uv run --with pandas --with numpy --with pyarrow python bench_pandas.py) done The figures above were taken before Parquet moved to parquetio. The Parquet code itself did not change in the split, only its package.
data.operations-on-a-table#Operations on a ta:
The table is built identically, value for value, by bench_test.go and bench/bench_pandas.py: key int64 in [0, 1000), x and y float64 in [0, 1), cat a string among 100 values. Operations:
groupby_sum: df.groupby("key").sum() — GroupBy("key").Sum() groupby_sum_string: the same, keyed by the string column sort_values: stable sort by x (pandas kind="stable", polars maintain_order=True) filter: df[df.x > 0.5] merge: inner join with a 1000-row table on key (unique on the right) memory: bytes the table holds (Go: heap growth when building it; pandas: memory_usage(deep=True); polars: estimated_size()) Reproduce: sh bench/run.sh 1000000 5 > out.txt && python3 bench/medians.py out.txt.
data.reading#Reading: Against pandas’ default C parser: about 10× faster (9.9× at 10^6, 10.4× at 10^7), and 10–16× with dates parsed. Against polars: within 5% at 10^6 and about 13% slower at 10^7 on the default read; level (within noise) with dates. Faster than pandas' pyarrow engine on every run but one. Memory: the peak resident size of a read is in line with pandas and polars (lower once their interpreter baseline is counted), but the frame read holds about 2× pandas’ and 2.8× polars’ bytes, because the strings share the input buffer and Go strings carry 16-byte headers. That is the price of zero-copy strings; see docs/design.md (CSV section). Go benchmarks (go test -bench 'ReadCSV|WriteCSV', in-memory, same table shape, load ~35): ReadCSV 10^6 rows ≈ 40–48 ms (≈1.1–1.3 GB/s); WriteCSV 10^5 rows ≈ 14 ms (≈400 MB/s).
data.reading-these-honestly#Reading these hon: Against pandas: sorting is about 2x faster (stable LSD radix sort), merge 1.3–1.7x, group-by on an int key at parity to 2x, group-by on a string key and the filter at parity or better. Nothing measured is slower than pandas by more than noise, except the string group-by in run A at 10^7, before factorisation went parallel. Against polars: polars is faster on most operations on a quiet machine (2–4x on filter, merge and string group-by); sorting is close. Memory is the weak point. Numeric columns cost what pandas’ cost (8 bytes a value). A string column is a Go []string: 16 bytes of header per value, plus the bytes (shared here, since there are only 100 distinct values). pandas 3 and polars store strings Arrow-style (offsets + one byte buffer), about 11 bytes a value here — so this table is 40 MB here against 35 MB in pandas and 27 MB in polars. Converting such a column to Category (4 bytes a value) makes it the smallest of the three. An Arrow-style string column is the obvious next step. The merge benchmark joins on keys unique on the right with every left row matched, so the left columns are shared rather than gathered (columns are immutable); a join that duplicates or drops left rows gathers them. Go’s garbage collector scans []string columns; with large string columns a share of the time in allocation-heavy operations (filter, merge) is GC.

data.setup#Setup:
Frame. Six columns, built identically on both sides (benchFrame in arrowio/bench_test.go, for IPC, and in parquetio/bench_test.go, for Parquet; arrowio/testdata/bench_pandas.py on the pandas side):
column type missing float64 float64 1% NaN int64 int64 none string 1,000 distinct values 1% category 10 levels none bool bool none datetime datetime none Operations.
Parquet with Snappy compression, the default on both sides. parquetio produces a 15.2 MB file. The Arrow IPC file format without compression. For pandas this is to_feather(compression="uncompressed"). Method.
7 runs, with Go and pandas interleaved: a Go run, then a pandas run, and so on. Each run reports the mean of 3 repetitions of each operation, in milliseconds. The table gives the median of the 7 runs. Machine. Apple M4 Max, 16 cores. The host is shared and was loaded throughout: uptime load averages were 14.97 / 18.50 / 18.88 before the runs and 14.15 / 17.96 / 18.67 after.
Versions. Go 1.27.2, apache/arrow-go v18.8.0. pandas 3.0.6, pyarrow 26.0.0, Python 3.12.12.
data.where-the-time-goes#Where the time goes:
Parquet write. About 70% of the allocations happen in arrow-go’s dictionary encoder for byte arrays: hashing.(*BinaryMemoTable).InsertOrGet makes about one allocation per string value (1.0 M allocations per write of the 10^6-row frame). pyarrow uses the same encoding, with dictionaries on by default, but in C++. Our conversion itself shares the numeric buffers and adds one pass for strings.
Parquet read. The time is dominated by arrow-go’s column decoding, which runs in parallel across columns. Our conversion is a minority of the profile:
copying the validity bitmaps (with bitutil.CopyBitmap) one copy of each numeric buffer into the frame’s own array one string allocation per chunk for the text IPC read. pyarrow’s to_pandas is mostly zero-copy for numeric columns, so pandas pays almost nothing to read them. We copy every column once into storage the frame owns, because go-ndarray cannot adopt foreign memory. The string column also gets its []string headers built, and then copied once more by the core’s constructor.
IPC write. This is zero-copy for numeric and datetime columns, which is why it beats pandas.
data.where-the-time-goes-profile-107-rows#Whe: About half the CPU is the first conversion pass (integer and float parsing; strconv.ParseFloat for 17-digit values), a fifth the tokenizer, an eighth building the string columns, and a tenth the garbage collector marking the string columns. The remaining gap to polars is mostly float parsing (an Eisel–Lemire parser of our own would skip ParseFloat’s re-scan) and GC work on string headers.

data:
dataframe/dfplot draws a frame with go-plot: one line per column against the index, as df.plot() does, and Bar, Barh, Hist, Area, Scatter and the Series variants. The legend names the columns and the x label is the name of the index; a missing value breaks a line. Each function returns a *plot.Figure, which saves as SVG or PNG and shows in a notebook through Display.
Every figure on this page was drawn by go-dataframe v0.1.0 and go-plot v0.1.0 from the code shown under it; the CI draws it again and fails if one byte of the SVG differs.

package main import ( "github.com/go-dataframe/dataframe" "github.com/go-dataframe/dataframe/dfplot" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("bars", bars) } // df.groupby("city")[["rain"]].mean().plot.bar() func bars() *plot.Figure { g := dataframe.Must(rainfall().GroupBy("city")) means := dataframe.Must(g.Mean()) fig, err := dfplot.BarOpts(means, []string{"rain"}, []dfplot.Option{dfplot.WithTitle("Mean yearly rainfall, 2022–2024 (mm)")}) if err != nil { panic(err) } return fig } The data, shared with the notebook display page:
package main import "github.com/go-dataframe/dataframe" // rainfall is the table the examples share: yearly rainfall in millimetres and // rainy days at three stations. The numbers are made up for the example. func rainfall() *dataframe.DataFrame { return dataframe.Must(dataframe.New( dataframe.Col("city", []string{"Lyon", "Paris", "Nice", "Lyon", "Paris", "Nice", "Lyon", "Paris", "Nice"}), dataframe.Col("year", []int{2022, 2022, 2022, 2023, 2023, 2023, 2024, 2024, 2024}), dataframe.Col("rain", []float64{741.2, 512.9, 698.4, 830.5, 640.2, 702.3, 810.0, 598.7, 760.1}), dataframe.Col("days", []int{98, 103, 61, 112, 118, 64, 107, 111, 70}), )) }
data.lines-and-a-rolling-mean#Lines, and a ro: package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-dataframe/dataframe" "github.com/go-dataframe/dataframe/dfplot" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("lines", lines) } // Sixty days of a made-up daily temperature, and its 7-day rolling mean: // s.rolling(7).mean(), then df.plot(). The first six means are missing, // as in pandas, and the line starts at day 7. func lines() *plot.Figure { day := make([]int, 60) temp := make([]float64, 60) for i := range day { day[i] = i + 1 temp[i] = 12 + 6*math.Sin(2*math.Pi*float64(i)/60) + 2.5*math.Sin(1.7*float64(i)) } s := dataframe.Must(dataframe.NewSeries("temperature", temp)) r := dataframe.Must(s.Rolling(7)) df := dataframe.Must(dataframe.New( dataframe.Col("day", day), dataframe.Col("temperature", s), dataframe.Col("7-day mean", r.Mean()), )) df = dataframe.Must(df.SetIndex("day")) fig, err := dfplot.LineOpts(df, nil, []dfplot.Option{dfplot.WithTitle("Daily temperature (°C)")}) if err != nil { panic(err) } return fig }
